source_units.text:
## Prerequisites and checks

### O001-P1

`item_id: O001-P1`, `item_version: 1`, role: prerequisite diagnostic. Capability: local; reason: Separate a document report from a verified live instruction.

Prompt: If two supplied documents disagree on a deadline, does the newer file name establish the deadline?

Key: No. Record both statements and ask for the actual assignment instructions/course-team clarification; timestamps/file names do not resolve the conflict.

Rubric: pass only if the stated answer and its essential reason are correct without help; partial for incomplete reasoning or a recoverable arithmetic slip; fail for a contrary concept or no usable answer. This diagnostic never counts toward acquisition. Repair: Use the distinction explained in Motivation, intuition, and definitions, then the supported task.

Adequate committed current-version evidence for the named capability permits skipping that diagnostic; familiarity/confidence does not. If there is no evidence, ask each diagnostic once. Local foundation failures use the exact explanation here, not an improvised prerequisite curriculum.

## Motivation, intuition, and definitions

Produce a reliable preparation/submission checklist from the supplied course introduction, distinguish confirmed common requirements from unresolved differences, and delimit the academic scope actually prepared. The question is what the available information lets us calculate or conclude, and which extra conditions the conclusion needs.

The supplied syllabus/catalog identify JEB110, 6 ECTS, and Econometrics I (JEB109) as a prerequisite. Course purpose is independent empirical work: question → equation/data → estimate → assumptions → interpretation/report. R is official seminar software. Uploaded readings recommend Wooldridge; Week 1 refers to Chapters 2 and 5. The historical Week1 snapshot did not ingest Chapter10. Historical P003 separately prepared the bounded checked Week2 finite-sample time-series, FDL, trend and seasonal mechanisms in O009–O013. source_units.heading: Explanation steps
source_units.text:
## Explanation steps

1. Separate assessment components: four assignments ×10 =40, midterm 20, final 40, maximum total 100.
2. Apply the separate final gate: more than 20 out of 40; at integer scores this is at least 21. A high overall total cannot substitute for this gate.
3. Preserve submission wording: theoretical plus empirical small project/report, group solution naming both participants, appended R code and no late credit per syllabus. Lecture says groups of two and permits other software; syllabus/catalog encourage pairs and request R code. Individual submissions and other-software acceptance therefore require clarification.
4. Maintain a discrepancy list rather than averaging documents: HA1 October 19 versus October 26; fractional/integer grade bands and gaps; impossible September 31; unclear midterm end time. Uploaded documents agree on November 11 at 12:30 as the midterm start, but this lesson creates no event.
5. Midterm: first six lectures, multiple-choice/YES–NO; final: whole course, theoretical and practical questions. This is exam-format context, while the historical Week1 snapshot prepared only its introductory scope. The historical Week1 snapshot did not ingest Chapter10. Historical P003 separately prepared the bounded checked Week2 finite-sample time-series, FDL, trend and seasonal mechanisms in O009–O013. Full later Chapter11 and the whole reported exam scope remain uncovered; no learner mastery is inferred. The final has up to three trials in the lecture; both exams are compulsory/in person in the catalog.
6. Preparation sequence is revisit OLS, use current ready Week1 and bounded Week2 lessons, then obtain and ingest unsupported later material. Do not infer later-topic mastery or coverage.

Current P004 additionally prepares the checked bounded Week3 process and asymptotic material in O014–O019; full Chapter11 and later advertised methods remain excluded.

### Course purpose and preparation

This is the second undergraduate econometrics course. Its purpose is to enable independent empirical work: translate a research question into a regression equation, select a data structure and method, estimate it in statistical software, assess the assumptions, and interpret the results. The lecture emphasizes understanding the data-generating process because economic data do not automatically meet the assumptions of an exact statistical model. The SIS export lists 6 ECTS, Econometrics I (JEB109) as a prerequisite, and JEB125 as a course for which this course is a prerequisite. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=10|Lecture 1, PDF pp. 10–12]]; [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Předměty.pdf#page=1|SIS export, PDF p. 1]]

The lecturer is Barbara Pertold-Gebicka; the seminar leaders are Veronika Plachá, Oliver Škultéty, and Kai Wang. The uploaded schedule gives Wednesday lectures at 12:30–13:50 and seminars on Wednesday at 15:30–16:50 or 18:30–19:50, or Thursday at 14:00–15:20. The lecture lists room 016 for seminars. Prepare by reading the assigned material and revising prerequisite methods before the lecture or seminar. Week 1's lecture is September 30, and the seminar handout is dated September 30 / October 1, 2026. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=2|Lecture 1, PDF pp. 2, 5, 12]]; [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Syllabus_2026.pdf#page=1|Syllabus 2026, PDF pp. 1–2]]; [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Seminar 1 OS/Seminar1.pdf#page=1|Seminar 1, PDF p. 1, header]]

The main textbook is Jeffrey M. Wooldridge's *Introductory Econometrics: A Modern Approach*, fourth edition or higher according to the lecture. The lecture recommends Chris Brooks, Angrist and Pischke, and Cameron and Trivedi as complementary readings; the SIS export lists Brooks and Cameron and Trivedi. These are reading references, not sources ingested in this pass. R is the official seminar software. The lecture permits other software in home assignments, while the syllabus and SIS export request appended R code; students should clarify expectations if using another package. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=4|Lecture 1, PDF pp. 4, 7]]; [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Syllabus_2026.pdf#page=1|Syllabus 2026, PDF p. 1]]; [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Předměty.pdf#page=2|SIS export, PDF p. 2]]

### Assessment and submitted work

Four assignments are worth up to 10 points each (40 total), the midterm up to 20, and the final up to 40. Passing requires more than 20 final-exam points; the lecture expresses this as at least 21 points and more than 50% of the final. A good overall total cannot replace this separate final-exam requirement. The midterm is one-shot; the lecture gives November 11, 2026, at 12:30. The final takes place in the exam period, and the lecture permits three trials. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=6|Lecture 1, PDF pp. 6, 9]]; [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Syllabus_2026.pdf#page=2|Syllabus 2026, PDF p. 2]]

Assignments combine a theoretical problem and an empirical problem treated as a small project with a short report. Lecture 1 says “Work in groups of 2 students,” whereas the syllabus and SIS export encourage groups of two; the source wording differs in whether pairing is expressed as a requirement or encouragement. The syllabus says each such group submits one solution naming both participants, appends R code, and meets the stated deadline because late work receives no credit. The lecture promises assignment feedback within 10 working days and exam scores within 7 working days. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=7|Lecture 1, PDF pp. 7–9]]; [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Syllabus_2026.pdf#page=1|Syllabus 2026, PDF p. 1]]

The midterm uses multiple-choice and YES/NO questions according to Lecture 1. Its stated scope is the first six lectures, testing theoretical and practical knowledge. The final covers the whole course and includes true/false, open theoretical, and open practical questions. The SIS export explicitly describes both exams as compulsory and in person. These statements record the supplied exam formats and scope; they do not ingest the later lecture content. ### Boundary of this Week 1 ingestion

The syllabus and SIS export identify Week 1 as unbiasedness, consistency, and efficiency, with Wooldridge Chapters 2 and 5. The lecture asks students to revise cross-sectional OLS assumptions and properties and read Chapter 10 before the next lecture. This is a preparation instruction, not ingested Chapter 10 content. ## Rubric and independence

Pass: all C1–C4 correct, essential reasoning explicit, known independent conditions and fresh item. Partial: one or more components missing, an unexplained claim, or a recoverable arithmetic slip with sound method. source_units.heading: Motivation, intuition, and definitions
source_units.text:
## Motivation, intuition, and definitions

Derive the OLS normal equations and centered solution, calculate fitted values/residuals, use matrix dimensions/full rank, and distinguish algebraic fitting identities from population assumptions. The question is what the available information lets us calculate or conclude, and which extra conditions the conclusion needs.

Population model $y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1 x_i+u_i$: fixed population parameters, generally unobserved disturbance. Hats mark sample estimates; $\hat u_i=y_i-\hat y_i$ is an observable fitted residual. Slope units are y units per x unit; intercept at x=0 needs substantive relevance. $S_{xx}=\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2$, $S_{xy}=\sum(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)$. In multiple regression X includes ones; k counts nonconstant regressors. OLS can be calculated without certifying a causal relationship.

source_units.heading: Explanation steps
source_units.text:
## Explanation steps

1. Minimize $Q(b)=\sum(y_i-b_0-b_1 x_i)^2$. Derivatives are $-2\sum\hat u_i$ and $-2\sum x_i\hat u_i$; set both to zero.
2. The first implies $b_0=\bar y-b_1\bar x$. Substitute into the second: $S_{xy}-b_1 S_{xx}=0$, giving $\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}$ and $\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x$ if $S_{xx}>0$. Centering makes $\sum(x_i-\bar x)=0$.
3. Predictions are $\hat y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1 x_i$; residuals are actual minus fitted. Thus positive residual means actual exceeds prediction. Intercept OLS yields $\sum\hat u_i=\sum x_i\hat u_i=0$ as minimization identities; it does not yield $E[u\mid x]=0$.
4. For $y=X\beta+u$, dimensions are y, u:n×1; X:n×(k +1); beta:(k +1)×1. Normal equations $X'X\hat\beta=X'y$ have (k +1)×(k +1) multiplying (k +1)×1. Full column rank makes the inverse available and yields $(X'X)^{-1}X'y=\beta+(X'X)^{-1}X'u$. The equations estimate all coefficients jointly; separate simple regressions do not hold the other variables fixed.
5. Name the assumption ladder: linear in parameters, random sampling, no perfect collinearity, zero conditional mean, homoskedasticity, conditional normality. A squared/transformed regressor can still be linear in parameters. Algebra needs full rank for uniqueness; sampling properties need additional named assumptions. Zero population conditional mean is about disturbances, not fitted residuals.

source_units.text:
## Complete checked-note explanation

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/OLS_Estimator_and_Assumptions.md#OLS estimator and assumptions]]; fingerprint `8e76f95b0071e8625c31230e9c96e2a738e7d88251b1ba978d0bc35225fc380a`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### OLS estimator and assumptions

How does a regression coefficient relate an observed sample to the population relationship we want to study? Week 1 revises ordinary least squares (OLS), then asks which assumptions make its coefficients trustworthy. The formula is a sample calculation; unbiasedness, consistency, and efficiency are properties that require a model of how the data were generated. This distinction prepares the course's later extensions to other data structures. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=10|Lecture 1, PDF pp. 10–11]]

Back to [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Econometrics_II_main#Week 1|Econometrics II — Week 1]].

#### Population model, sample, and notation

The lecture uses the simple population regression

$$
y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+u_i,\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
$$

Here $i$ labels an observation, $n$ is the sample size, $y_i$ is the dependent variable, and $x_i$ is one explanatory variable. The population parameters $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ describe the intercept and slope. The disturbance $u_i$ collects the variation in $y_i$ that the specified systematic part does not explain. A hat indicates a sample estimator or its realized estimate, so $\hat\beta_1$ differs conceptually from the fixed population parameter $\beta_1$. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=14|Lecture 1, PDF pp. 14–15]]

The slope measures the change in the systematic part of $y$ associated with a one-unit change in $x$. Its units are units of $y$ per unit of $x$. The intercept is the systematic value at $x=0$; interpreting it substantively requires that zero be meaningful and relevant to the data. A causal interpretation of the slope requires appropriate assumptions about the disturbance and regressor; the existence of a fitted line by itself does not establish causation. These interpretations unpack the model used in the lecture and the units-and-parameters task in the seminar. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=14|Lecture 1, PDF p. 14]]; [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Seminar 1 OS/Seminar1.pdf#page=1|Seminar 1, PDF p. 1, Problem 1(ii)]]

#### How OLS chooses the line

**Algebraic explanation of the lecture's estimator.** OLS selects coefficients $b_0,b_1$ to minimize the sum of squared residuals,

$$
Q(b_0,b_1)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i)^2.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $b_0$ and $b_1$ gives the two normal equations: $\sum_i(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i)=0$ and $\sum_ix_i(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i)=0$. The first equation implies $b_0=\bar y-b_1\bar x$. Substituting this into the second equation produces the centered formula shown in the lecture:

$$
\hat\beta_1=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}
=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}
{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2},
\qquad
\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x.
$$

The bars denote sample means. The numerator measures how $x$ and $y$ vary together around their means; the denominator measures the sample variation available in $x$. The slope therefore compares co-movement with regressor variation. If every $x_i$ is identical, $S_{xx}=0$, so the data cannot distinguish the slope from the intercept. The minimization steps are an agent explanation of the displayed source formula, rather than additional lecture slides. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=15|Lecture 1, PDF p. 15]]

The fitted value is $\hat y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i$ and the residual is $\hat u_i=y_i-\hat y_i$. Residuals are observable after estimation; population disturbances are generally unobserved. With an intercept, the normal equations ensure $\sum_i\hat u_i=0$ and $\sum_ix_i\hat u_i=0$. These are fitting identities and do **not** establish the population exogeneity assumption $E[u_i\mid x_i]=0$. The seminar asks for residuals precisely because they can be calculated from the observed data and fitted line. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Seminar 1 OS/Seminar1.pdf#page=1|Seminar 1, PDF p. 1, Problem 1(iv)]]; [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=18|Lecture 1, PDF p. 18]]

#### The assumption ladder

The lecture uses Wooldridge's numbering. State the assumptions by name as well as number, because different textbooks number them differently. The following notation makes the lecture's named assumptions explicit. For multiple regression let $x_i=(x_{i1},\ldots,x_{ik})$ contain the $k$ nonconstant regressors, and let $X$ denote the full sample design, including an intercept. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=18|Lecture 1, PDF p. 18]]; [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=25|Lecture 1, PDF p. 25]]

| Assumption | Meaning and role |
|---|---|
| Linear in parameters (MLR.1) | $y_i=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^k\beta_jx_{ij}+u_i$. Linearity refers to the coefficients: a regressor can itself be a transformation, provided the specified model remains linear in its parameters. This supplies the decomposition used in the estimator proofs. |
| Random sampling (MLR.2) | Observations are independent draws from the population under study. The lecture emphasizes representativeness and independence. This justifies the cross-sectional sampling argument and the law-of-large-numbers reasoning used later. A convenience sample is not made representative by running OLS. |
| No perfect collinearity (MLR.3) | No regressor is an exact linear combination of the others, and each nonconstant regressor has variation. In simple regression this requires $S_{xx}>0$; in multiple regression it makes the design matrix full rank. Otherwise coefficients cannot be uniquely separated. |
| Zero conditional mean (MLR.4) | $E[u_i\mid x_{i1},\ldots,x_{ik}]=0$. Once the included regressors are fixed, the average disturbance is zero. Under the sampling assumptions this yields $E[u_i\mid X]=0$ in the source's conditional proof. |
| Homoskedasticity (MLR.5) | $\operatorname{Var}(u_i\mid x_i)=\sigma^2$, a constant finite variance. With the preceding assumptions, this establishes the Gauss–Markov efficiency result. |
| Normality (MLR.6) | The disturbance has a conditional normal distribution; together with the preceding assumptions, this gives normal conditional coefficient distributions and exact null $t$ and $F$ distributions. |

The lecture introduces the first four assumptions for unbiasedness, adds homoskedasticity for BLUE, and adds normality for classical finite-sample inference. The formal statements here explain that sequence; they should not be read as claims that the seminar data automatically satisfy it. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=16|Lecture 1, PDF pp. 16–19]]; [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=23|Lecture 1, PDF pp. 23–26]]

#### Why multiple regression uses matrix notation

The lecture asks why matrix notation is more convenient when there is more than one regressor. **Agent explanation:** write $y=X\beta+u$, where $y$ and $u$ are $n\times1$ vectors, $X$ is $n\times(k+1)$, and $\beta$ is $(k+1)\times1$. Its first column is ones. Minimizing $(y-Xb)'(y-Xb)$ yields $X'X\hat\beta=X'y$. If $X$ has full column rank,

$$
\hat\beta=(X'X)^{-1}X'y
=\beta+(X'X)^{-1}X'u.
$$

The prime means transpose. The inverse exists under no perfect collinearity. This single expression handles every coefficient jointly, instead of treating each regressor as a separate simple regression. Joint estimation matters because the slope for a regressor holds the other included regressors fixed; omitting them generally changes the comparison being made. This is the extension requested in the seminar's alternative-specification table. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=15|Lecture 1, PDF p. 15, matrix-notation question]]; [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Seminar 1 OS/Seminar1.pdf#page=2|Seminar 1, PDF p. 2, Problem 1(vi)–(vii)]]

#### What to carry forward

OLS always describes a calculation once the data and specification are fixed. The assumption ladder determines what can be concluded about repeated samples, large samples, relative precision, and hypothesis tests. [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Unbiasedness_Consistency_and_Efficiency|Unbiasedness, consistency, and efficiency]] proves these distinctions using the estimator's disturbance term. [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Transport_Demand_Regression_Seminar|The transport-demand seminar]] applies the calculation and shows why a change in controls can change the estimated price relationship.

## Worked example

O002-W v1, hypothetical x=(1,2,3), y=(2,3,7): means 2 and 4; Sxx 2; Sxy=(-1)(-2)+0(-1)+(1)(3)=5. Slope 2.5, intercept -1. Predictions 1.5,4,6.5, residuals 0.5,-1,0.5; sum 0 and x-weighted sum 0. The line passes through(2,4); this checks intercept arithmetic. Slope 2.5 y units per x unit; zero-x intercept is outside observations. For n=20, k=2, X is 20×3, $X'X$ 3×3; a regressor equal to twice another makes X rank deficient, so the inverse formula cannot be used. No sample identity establishes exogeneity.

Role: complete demonstration, never independent evidence. Unless explicitly identified as a finished-note result, numerical/context examples are agent-created hypothetical instantiations of the note-supported mechanism.

source_units.text:
## Rubric and independence

Pass: all C1–C4 correct, essential reasoning explicit, known independent conditions and fresh item. Partial: one or more components missing, an unexplained claim, or a recoverable arithmetic slip with sound method. Fail: a critical conceptual error, wrong method/assumptions/interpretation, or no usable attempt. Unscorable: unknown conditions/exposure or an alternative outside the prepared key. Equivalent algebra, clear verbal reasoning and synonymous units/assumption names are acceptable; assumption numbers alone are insufficient. Numerical rounding to sensible precision is acceptable. A isolated arithmetic slip is partial and is not treated as established conceptual failure; the learner must independently repair it with a fresh prepared full item before a pass qualifies. No numeric grading scale is invented.

Every full task I1, I2, D1, D2 expressly requests all C1–C4 and has a complete task-specific key plus exact conceptual reasoning above. Omitted pieces are partial even if an unasked answer happens to sound fluent. Supported S and narrow correction C never substitute for a full check.

Any selected pair of distinct items from {I1,I2,D1,D2} covers C1–C4 twice. Do not use an item twice or count a corrected answer to the same item as fresh. D items used immediately are logged as independent replacement checks, not delayed evidence. No shortened variant or arbitrary new task is permitted. Two complete unassisted passes under O002-C1 establish acquisition; they do not establish retention. This is a default evidence rule, not a learner outcome.

source_units.heading: Misconceptions and correction
source_units.text:
## Misconceptions and correction

Sign: using uncentered $\sum xy/\sum x^2$ despite an intercept, reversing residual sign, or calling zero residual correlation exogeneity. Correction: the intercept is eliminated through sample means; use actual minus fitted; OLS forces orthogonality regardless of population disturbance relation. Hint1: isolate the intercept with the first normal equation. Hint2: substitute the centered form into the second.

Score the original response before help. One ambiguous error only suggests a tentative misconception; establish it only from explicit reasoning or repeated diagnostic signs. Explain the relevant prepared step and its consequence; never label the learner from confidence or a single slip.

### O002-C

`item_id: O002-C`, `item_version: 1`, role: targeted correction; not an acquisition substitute.

Prompt: Fresh O002-C v1: x=(1,2), y=(4,8). Give line/residuals and explain whether a perfect fit proves exogeneity.

Key: Means 1.5,6; Sxx 0.5, Sxy 2; slope 4/intercept 0; residual 0,0. Perfect sample fit does not establish population exogeneity. This targets centering/identity only; it is not a complete substitute.

Rubric: correct supplied answer plus the exact boundary/reason is a repair pass; omitted reason is partial; repeating the original misconception is fail. Repair success licenses returning to a fresh full prepared item; it never replaces full C1–C4 coverage.

source_units.heading: Motivation, intuition, and definitions
source_units.text:
## Motivation, intuition, and definitions

Derive the slope disturbance decomposition and conditional/unconditional mean, identify the role of each first four assumption, and explain the limits of repeated-sample unbiasedness. The question is what the available information lets us calculate or conclude, and which extra conditions the conclusion needs.

Unbiasedness means $E[\hat\beta_j]=\beta_j$ across repeated samples. Conditioning on X fixes weights/denominator. It does not fix disturbances or set each realized disturbance to zero. The first four named assumptions suffice; homoskedasticity and normality are not required for this mean result.

source_units.heading: Explanation steps
source_units.text:
## Explanation steps

1. From the linear population equation subtract sample means: $y_i-\bar y=\beta_1(x_i-\bar x)+(u_i-\bar u)$.
2. Insert into $S_{xy}/S_{xx}$; cancel beta 1*Sxx/Sxx. Since centered x sums0, the term involving ubar vanishes: $\hat\beta_1=\beta_1+\sum(x_i-\bar x)u_i/S_{xx}$.
3. Conditional on the whole sample X, Sxx and centered weights are fixed. Thus $E[\hat\beta_1\mid X]=\beta_1+S_{xx}^{-1}\sum(x_i-\bar x)E[u_i\mid X]$. Random sampling plus observation-level zero conditional mean supply $E[u_i\mid X]=0$.
4. The mean error term is 0. Iterated expectation gives $E[\hat\beta_1]=E[E[\hat\beta_1\mid X]]=\beta_1$. For all coefficients, the note's matrix decomposition gives the same conditional argument $E[\hat\beta\mid X]=\beta+(X'X)^{-1}X'E[u\mid X]=\beta$.
5. Linear parameters allow decomposition; random sampling supports conditioning on the full sample; no perfect collinearity allows finite inverse/positive denominator; zero conditional mean eliminates mean errors. Homoskedasticity controls variance, not this mean; normality supports exact inference later.
6. Realized estimation error generally remains nonzero. An unbiased estimator can have large dispersion; one coefficient, residual orthogonality or a high fit cannot certify its repeated-sample property.

source_units.heading: Complete checked-note explanation
source_units.text:
## Complete checked-note explanation

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Unbiasedness_Consistency_and_Efficiency.md#One decomposition drives both proofs]]; fingerprint `afc4f90940a6f9e889acff6e5e1194c5fde424636cbfca31f540eee2c5051595`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### One decomposition drives both proofs

For $y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+u_i$, centering gives $y_i-\bar y=\beta_1(x_i-\bar x)+(u_i-\bar u)$. Substitute this into the OLS numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat\beta_1
&=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)[\beta_1(x_i-\bar x)+(u_i-\bar u)]}{S_{xx}}\\
&=\beta_1+\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(u_i-\bar u)}{S_{xx}}\\
&=\beta_1+\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)u_i}{S_{xx}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The final step uses $\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0$, so subtracting $\bar u$ changes nothing. This algebra identifies the estimation error: sample co-movement between the regressor and disturbance, divided by sample regressor variation. The lecture uses the uncentered-disturbance version for unbiasedness and the centered version for consistency. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=19|Lecture 1, PDF p. 19]]; [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=22|Lecture 1, PDF p. 22]]


Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Unbiasedness_Consistency_and_Efficiency.md#Unbiasedness: the repeated-sample average]]; fingerprint `afc4f90940a6f9e889acff6e5e1194c5fde424636cbfca31f540eee2c5051595`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Unbiasedness: the repeated-sample average

An estimator is unbiased when $E[\hat\beta_j]=\beta_j$. Expectation refers to repeated sampling from the population under the model, not to averaging different coefficients from a single fitted regression. The lecture's theorem states that the linear-in-parameters, random-sampling, no-perfect-collinearity, and zero-conditional-mean assumptions imply unbiasedness for all OLS coefficients. Homoskedasticity and normality are not required for this result. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=16|Lecture 1, PDF pp. 16–18]]

To see the role of exogeneity, condition on the observed regressor sample $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$. Then $S_{xx}$ and the weights $x_i-\bar x$ are fixed. Linearity of conditional expectation gives

$$
E[\hat\beta_1\mid X]
=\beta_1+\frac{1}{S_{xx}}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)E[u_i\mid X]
=\beta_1.
$$

The zero-conditional-mean assumption, together with random sampling, supplies $E[u_i\mid X]=0$. Taking expectation again gives $E[\hat\beta_1]=E[E[\hat\beta_1\mid X]]=\beta_1$. Linearity of the model supplies the initial decomposition; no perfect collinearity makes the denominator positive; random sampling supports the move from observation-level exogeneity to conditioning on the full sample design. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=19|Lecture 1, PDF p. 19, conditional-expectation derivation]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/assets/lecture1_p19_unbiasedness_derivation.png]]

*Source crop: Lecture 1, PDF p. 19. The weights and denominator can leave the conditional expectation because $X$ is held fixed; exogeneity makes the remaining conditional disturbance means zero.* [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=19|Source, PDF p. 19]]

Unbiasedness means there is no systematic overestimation or underestimation across repeated samples. It does not guarantee that the estimate from a particular sample is close to the truth: dispersion can be large even when its center is correct. That is why precision and consistency are separate questions. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=17|Lecture 1, PDF p. 17]]


Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/OLS_Estimator_and_Assumptions.md#The assumption ladder]]; fingerprint `8e76f95b0071e8625c31230e9c96e2a738e7d88251b1ba978d0bc35225fc380a`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### The assumption ladder

The lecture uses Wooldridge's numbering. State the assumptions by name as well as number, because different textbooks number them differently. The following notation makes the lecture's named assumptions explicit. For multiple regression let $x_i=(x_{i1},\ldots,x_{ik})$ contain the $k$ nonconstant regressors, and let $X$ denote the full sample design, including an intercept. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=18|Lecture 1, PDF p. 18]]; [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=25|Lecture 1, PDF p. 25]]

| Assumption | Meaning and role |
|---|---|
| Linear in parameters (MLR.1) | $y_i=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^k\beta_jx_{ij}+u_i$. Linearity refers to the coefficients: a regressor can itself be a transformation, provided the specified model remains linear in its parameters. This supplies the decomposition used in the estimator proofs. |
| Random sampling (MLR.2) | Observations are independent draws from the population under study. The lecture emphasizes representativeness and independence. This justifies the cross-sectional sampling argument and the law-of-large-numbers reasoning used later. A convenience sample is not made representative by running OLS. |
| No perfect collinearity (MLR.3) | No regressor is an exact linear combination of the others, and each nonconstant regressor has variation. In simple regression this requires $S_{xx}>0$; in multiple regression it makes the design matrix full rank. Otherwise coefficients cannot be uniquely separated. |
| Zero conditional mean (MLR.4) | $E[u_i\mid x_{i1},\ldots,x_{ik}]=0$. Once the included regressors are fixed, the average disturbance is zero. Under the sampling assumptions this yields $E[u_i\mid X]=0$ in the source's conditional proof. |
| Homoskedasticity (MLR.5) | $\operatorname{Var}(u_i\mid x_i)=\sigma^2$, a constant finite variance. With the preceding assumptions, this establishes the Gauss–Markov efficiency result. |
| Normality (MLR.6) | The disturbance has a conditional normal distribution; together with the preceding assumptions, this gives normal conditional coefficient distributions and exact null $t$ and $F$ distributions. |

The lecture introduces the first four assumptions for unbiasedness, adds homoskedasticity for BLUE, and adds normality for classical finite-sample inference. The formal statements here explain that sequence; they should not be read as claims that the seminar data automatically satisfy it. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=16|Lecture 1, PDF pp. 16–19]]; [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=23|Lecture 1, PDF pp. 23–26]]

## Worked example

O003-W v1, hypothetical fixed X=(1,2,3), beta 1=2, Sxx 2. A realized u=(1,0,3) gives centered weighted sum(-1)(1)+0+(1)(3)=2; slope 3. This single error of +1 does not refute a model whose repeated-sample conditional u means are0. Under those mean assumptions E[slope|X]=2+(-1*0+0*0+1*0)/2=2, then E[slope]=2. Compare realized u with its conditional expectation: no step requires all realized u to vanish.

Role: complete demonstration, never independent evidence. Unless explicitly identified as a finished-note result, numerical/context examples are agent-created hypothetical instantiations of the note-supported mechanism.

`item_id: O003-S`, `item_version: 1`, role: supported_completion, condition: supported, relation: parallel_variant.

For X=(1,2,3), beta 1=2, Sxx 2, explain why realized weighted u sum 2 gives slope 3 but conditional means 0 give expected slope 2. Name the four assumptions and why no normality is required. Include the fixed-X matrix mean argument.

First four: linear parameters, random sampling, no perfect collinearity, zero conditional mean. Normality is irrelevant to setting the conditional mean 0; realization need not equal mean. source_units.text:
## Misconceptions and correction

Sign: expectation of ratio treated as ratio of expectations without conditioning, or claims unbiasedness makes each error0. Correction: fix X to make the denominator and weights constants; exogeneity sets conditional disturbance means, not realizations, to0. Hint1: what is fixed conditional on X? Hint2: rewrite the expectation as a weighted sum of E[ui|X].

Score the original response before help. One ambiguous error only suggests a tentative misconception; establish it only from explicit reasoning or repeated diagnostic signs. Explain the relevant prepared step and its consequence; never label the learner from confidence or a single slip.

### O003-C

`item_id: O003-C`, `item_version: 1`, role: targeted correction; not an acquisition substitute.

Prompt: Fresh O003-C v1: fixed centered x=(-2,0,2), Sxx 8, beta 1=5 and realized weighted u=-4. What are realized slope and conditional expected slope if E[u|X]=0?

Key: 4.5 and 5. The former uses actual weighted disturbances; the latter weighted conditional means 0. Narrow repair only.

Rubric: correct supplied answer plus the exact boundary/reason is a repair pass; omitted reason is partial; repeating the original misconception is fail. Repair success licenses returning to a fresh full prepared item; it never replaces full C1–C4 coverage.

source_units.heading: Motivation, intuition, and definitions
source_units.text:
## Motivation, intuition, and definitions

Derive the probability limit from centered OLS, state sampling/moment/nondegeneracy and orthogonality conditions, and discriminate finite-sample unbiasedness from concentration in probability. The question is what the available information lets us calculate or conclude, and which extra conditions the conclusion needs.

Consistency is $\hat\theta_n\to_p\theta$: for every fixed epsilon>0, P(|estimate-target|>epsilon)→0. It concerns a sequence indexed by n, not monotonic improvement of every realized sample. Probability limit names the value around which the sequence concentrates; it may differ from the intended parameter.

source_units.heading: Explanation steps
source_units.text:
## Explanation steps

1. Use $\hat\beta_1=\beta_1+\frac{n^{-1}\sum(x_i-\bar x)(u_i-\bar u)}{n^{-1}\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2}$, obtained by centered substitution and common division by n.
2. Under independent random sampling and finite moments sufficient for the law of large numbers, sample covariance tends to Cov(x, u), sample variance to Var(x). Require positive finite population Var(x) so the ratio is valid. Then plim slope = beta 1+$\operatorname{Cov}(x,u)/\operatorname{Var}(x)$.
3. If covariance0 the slope limit equals beta 1; otherwise larger samples concentrate at the wrong target. Zero conditional mean is sufficient, stronger than needed for these moments. The weaker condition is $E[u]=0$ for the intercept and $\operatorname{Cov}(x_j,u)=0$ for every nonconstant regressor, alongside other model/sampling/moment/rank conditions. $\operatorname{Cov}(1,u)=0$ says nothing about E[u].
4. Finite-sample unbiasedness concerns an expectation at each n. Consistency concerns concentration. Neither follows from one estimate or an unqualified large n.
5. For an unbiased sequence, Chebyshev bounds $P(|\widehat\theta-\theta|>\epsilon)\leq\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\theta)/\epsilon^2$; if variance→0, the probability bound→0. Unbiasedness alone does not require variance shrinkage. A finite-sample biased sequence can be consistent if error/bias disappears with n and its sampling error concentrates; do not infer consistency solely from decreasing bias without controlling dispersion.

source_units.heading: Complete checked-note explanation
source_units.text:
## Complete checked-note explanation

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Unbiasedness_Consistency_and_Efficiency.md#Consistency: concentration as sample size grows]]; fingerprint `afc4f90940a6f9e889acff6e5e1194c5fde424636cbfca31f540eee2c5051595`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Consistency: concentration as sample size grows

Consistency is convergence in probability: $\hat\beta_{j,n}\xrightarrow{p}\beta_j$. More explicitly, for every fixed tolerance $\varepsilon>0$,

$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}P(|\hat\beta_{j,n}-\beta_j|>\varepsilon)=0.
$$

The subscript $n$ emphasizes a sequence of estimators indexed by sample size. Consistency says that the probability of an error larger than any fixed tolerance approaches zero. It does not promise monotonic improvement for every realized sequence of samples. The lecture states OLS consistency under the first four assumptions and then shows that zero conditional mean is stronger than necessary for this particular large-sample result. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=20|Lecture 1, PDF pp. 20–21]]

#### Why population covariance determines the probability limit

Divide both parts of the disturbance ratio by $n$:

$$
\hat\beta_1=\beta_1+
\frac{n^{-1}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(u_i-\bar u)}
{n^{-1}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}.
$$

Under random sampling and finite moments sufficient for the law of large numbers, the numerator converges in probability to $\operatorname{Cov}(x,u)$ and the denominator to $\operatorname{Var}(x)$. With a positive finite population regressor variance, taking the ratio therefore gives

$$
\operatorname{plim}\hat\beta_1
=\beta_1+\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x,u)}{\operatorname{Var}(x)}.
$$

Here $\operatorname{plim}$ means probability limit. Finite moments and a nonzero limiting denominator are the regularity requirements needed to interpret the lecture's law-of-large-numbers step; the slide does not spell them out. If $\operatorname{Cov}(x,u)=0$, the additional term vanishes. If it is nonzero, more observations concentrate OLS around the wrong value. A larger sample therefore cannot by itself cure regressor–disturbance correlation. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=22|Lecture 1, PDF p. 22, probability-limit derivation]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/assets/lecture1_p22_consistency_derivation.png]]

*Source crop: Lecture 1, PDF p. 22. Centering and division by $n$ turn the estimation-error ratio into sample covariance over sample variance, which exposes its population limit.* [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=22|Source, PDF p. 22]]

#### A weaker exogeneity condition

For consistency, the lecture replaces zero conditional mean by the weaker conditions

$$
E[u]=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(x_j,u)=0\quad\text{for each nonconstant regressor }j=1,\ldots,k.
$$

The first condition handles the intercept, and the covariance conditions handle the slopes. The slide writes its index as $j=0,\ldots,k$; with a constant regressor $x_0=1$, its covariance with $u$ is automatically zero. This weaker condition, together with the other sampling, model, nondegeneracy, and moment conditions, supports consistency but need not imply finite-sample unbiasedness. Zero conditional mean implies these unconditional moments, whereas unconditional zero covariance need not imply a zero conditional mean at every regressor value. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=21|Lecture 1, PDF p. 21]]

#### How unbiasedness and consistency can differ

The lecture states that an unbiased estimator is consistent if its variance tends to zero. **Agent explanation:** when $E[\hat\theta_n]=\theta$, Chebyshev's inequality bounds $P(|\hat\theta_n-\theta|>\varepsilon)$ by $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_n)/\varepsilon^2$, so a vanishing variance implies convergence in probability. Unbiasedness alone does not control the variance. Conversely, finite-sample bias can vanish as $n$ grows, so a biased estimator can still be consistent. These are properties of the sampling sequence, not a classification that can be proved by examining one estimate. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=21|Lecture 1, PDF p. 21]]

## Misconceptions and correction

Sign: “large samples cure endogeneity”, “unbiased implies consistent”, or treating covariance0 as conditional mean 0. Correction: the LLN retains $\operatorname{Cov}(x,u)/\operatorname{Var}(x)$; concentration needs a correct limit, while finite-sample unbiasedness alone gives no shrinking-error guarantee. Hint1: identify numerator/denominator limits. Hint2: add their ratio to beta.

Score the original response before help. One ambiguous error only suggests a tentative misconception; establish it only from explicit reasoning or repeated diagnostic signs. Explain the relevant prepared step and its consequence; never label the learner from confidence or a single slip.

source_units.heading: Motivation, intuition, and definitions
source_units.text:
## Motivation, intuition, and definitions

Derive the simple-slope conditional variance, state the precise BLUE comparison class, calculate a conventional slope standard error/t statistic and degrees of freedom, and discriminate which assumptions support each property. The question is what the available information lets us calculate or conclude, and which extra conditions the conclusion needs.

BLUE means best linear unbiased estimator conditional on X. Linear means linear in y observations with X-determined weights; unbiased is the comparison restriction; best is minimum conditional variance within that class, coefficient by coefficient. It is not minimum variance among all estimators/all loss functions. Homoskedasticity is common finite conditional disturbance variance sigma². Normality is additional for the stated exact finite-sample null t/F distributions; F addresses joint coefficient restrictions, whose calculation is outside this bounded lesson.

source_units.heading: Explanation steps
source_units.text:
## Explanation steps

1. In the slope decomposition the error is a weighted sum of u with weights $(x_i-\bar x)/S_{xx}$. Variance of this sum has squared weight variance terms and cross-observation covariance terms.
2. Sampling conditions remove the cross terms; common conditional variance sigma² gives $Var(\hat\beta_1\mid X)=\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2\sigma^2/S_{xx}^2=\sigma^2/S_{xx}$. More x variation improves precision, more noise worsens it.
3. With MLR1–5, the Gauss–Markov theorem gives BLUE in the stated linear unbiased class; this explanation calculates OLS variance, not a full proof of the theorem. No normality needed for BLUE.
4. Estimate unknown sigma² by SSE/(n-k -1), giving simple-slope estimated variance hat-sigma²/Sxx and se its square root. k counts nonconstant regressors: residual df=n-k -1, not n-k.
5. For null beta 1,0 use t=(estimated slope-null)/se. Under the full six classical assumptions, compare to the t distribution with those df for exact finite-sample inference. Rejecting a zero slope does not establish exogeneity/causality. An F test addresses joint restrictions; no joint-test arithmetic is claimed without further prepared notes.
6. With heteroskedasticity but first four assumptions maintained, unbiasedness survives and consistency may survive with regularity; stated BLUE/conventional variance and exact classical t claims no longer follow. With MLR1–5 but nonnormality, BLUE still holds while the stated exact classical normal/t/F distributions are not established. This lesson supplies no unsupported replacement variance/test method.

source_units.text:
## Complete checked-note explanation

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Unbiasedness_Consistency_and_Efficiency.md#Efficiency: specify the comparison class]]; fingerprint `afc4f90940a6f9e889acff6e5e1194c5fde424636cbfca31f540eee2c5051595`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Efficiency: specify the comparison class

The Gauss–Markov theorem says that under linearity in parameters, random sampling, no perfect collinearity, zero conditional mean, and homoskedasticity, OLS is **BLUE conditional on $X$**: the best linear unbiased estimator. “Linear” means linear in the dependent-variable observations, with weights determined by $X$. “Unbiased” restricts the comparison to estimators centered on the target parameter. “Best” means smallest conditional variance within that class, coefficient by coefficient. This does not claim that every conceivable estimator has a larger variance, or that OLS minimizes all possible loss functions. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=23|Lecture 1, PDF pp. 23–24]]

For the simple-regression slope, the decomposition provides an explanatory variance calculation. Under conditional independence and common disturbance variance $\sigma^2$,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1\mid X)
=\frac{1}{S_{xx}^2}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2\sigma^2
=\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}.
$$

Cross-observation covariance terms vanish under the sampling assumptions. More variation in $x$ supplies a more precise slope, while more disturbance variation reduces precision. This equation answers the seminar's slope-variance question and explains why homoskedasticity matters for the usual standard error. With heteroskedasticity, zero conditional mean can still preserve unbiasedness and suitable conditions can preserve consistency, but the stated BLUE theorem and conventional variance formula no longer follow. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=24|Lecture 1, PDF p. 24]]; [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Seminar 1 OS/Seminar1.pdf#page=2|Seminar 1, PDF p. 2, slope-variance task]]


Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Unbiasedness_Consistency_and_Efficiency.md#Normality and hypothesis tests add another requirement]]; fingerprint `afc4f90940a6f9e889acff6e5e1194c5fde424636cbfca31f540eee2c5051595`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Normality and hypothesis tests add another requirement

The lecture adds normality to the preceding assumptions to obtain a conditional normal distribution for OLS coefficients and exact null $t$ and $F$ distributions. This is a finite-sample inference statement, separate from unbiasedness, consistency, and BLUE. For a null slope value $\beta_{1,0}$,

$$
t=\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_{1,0}}{\operatorname{se}(\hat\beta_1)}.
$$

Under the classical assumptions, in a regression with $k$ nonconstant regressors this statistic has a $t$ distribution with $n-k-1$ residual degrees of freedom under the null. An $F$ statistic addresses joint coefficient restrictions. The formula and degrees of freedom are an agent expansion of the lecture's null-distribution statement, used in the seminar's requested slope test. A small standard error or a large absolute $t$ statistic cannot establish exogeneity; inference is conditional on the maintained model assumptions. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=25|Lecture 1, PDF pp. 25–26]]; [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Seminar 1 OS/Seminar1.pdf#page=2|Seminar 1, PDF p. 2]]

### Distinctions to retain

| Question | Property | Week 1 OLS conditions and qualification |
|---|---|---|
| Is the repeated-sample center correct? | Unbiasedness | First four assumptions; an individual estimate can still be far from the parameter. |
| Does error become improbable as $n$ grows? | Consistency | First four assumptions are sufficient with regularity; weaker orthogonality moments can replace zero conditional mean. |
| Is the estimator most precise in the stated class? | BLUE efficiency | First five assumptions; the class is linear unbiased estimators conditional on $X$. |
| Are the stated finite-sample null distributions exact? | Classical inference | First six assumptions; normality is an additional requirement. |

These distinctions summarize Lecture 1, PDF pp. 16–26. [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Transport_Demand_Regression_Seminar|The transport-demand seminar]] turns them into interpretation questions: fit the model, identify what the evidence measures, and assess which assumptions can plausibly support it.

## Practice with fading assistance

For S, show the setup and allow reference to Explanation steps; ask the learner to supply the missing calculations/decisions and reasons before feedback. One hint identifies the relevant definition/step; a second reveals the next operation. If two hints fail, show the key and repair. Fade to independent checks only after the learner can explain the completed method or a passed diagnostic supports skipping S.

### O005-S

`item_id: O005-S`, `item_version: 1`, role: supported_completion, condition: supported, relation: parallel_variant.

Prompt: Complete slope variance derivation, then use n 10, k 1, Sxx 8, SSE 128, slope -4, null 0 for df/sigma²/variance/se/t and 5% decision (cutoff 2.306 supplied). Define BLUE; explain what is preserved under heteroskedasticity and what normality adds. What does F test? Explain separately how doubling sigma² at fixed Sxx and doubling Sxx at fixed sigma² affect BOTH slope variance and standard error.

Required response components: Weighted-variance derivation with vanishing cross terms and correct noise/regressor-variation effects; BLUE class and first 4/5/6 distinctions stated precisely; Correct df, noise/slope variance, se and null-centered t with conditional decision; Significance/exogeneity distinction and F joint-restriction purpose.

Key and essential reasoning: Weights squared sum cancels one Sxx; sampling cross covariances 0/common variance yield sigma²/Sxx. df 8, sigma² 16, var 2, se 1.414214, t -2.828427, reject under MLR1–6. BLUE under 1–5 is smallest conditional variance among linear-in-y unbiased estimators with X fixed weights. Heteroskedasticity alone need not break unbiasedness/regularity-based consistency but stated BLUE/conventional variance/exact classical test fail to follow. Normality adds exact finite-sample conditional normal/t/F; F joint restrictions. From sigma²/Sxx: doubling noise variance sigma² doubles slope variance and multiplies SE by sqrt(2); doubling Sxx halves slope variance and divides SE by sqrt(2).

Task rubric: apply C1–C4 and the cross-task decision rule below. The proof/definition/condition steps in Explanation steps are the exact shared conceptual key, not optional extra credit. All four components are expressly requested above.

### O005-I1

`item_id: O005-I1`, `item_version: 1`, role: full_capability_check, condition: independent, relation: parallel_variant.

Prompt: Derive simple-slope variance and explain cross terms. Use hypothetical n 10, k 1, Sxx 4, SSE 32, slope -2, null 0 to compute df, estimated noise variance, slope variance, se, t and 5% decision with cutoff 2.306. Define BLUE precisely; compare MLR1–4 with heteroskedasticity, MLR1–5 without normality, and MLR1–6. Explain limits of statistical significance and purpose of F. Explain separately how doubling sigma² at fixed Sxx and doubling Sxx at fixed sigma² affect BOTH slope variance and standard error.

Required response components: Weighted-variance derivation with vanishing cross terms and correct noise/regressor-variation effects; BLUE class and first 4/5/6 distinctions stated precisely; Correct df, noise/slope variance, se and null-centered t with conditional decision; Significance/exogeneity distinction and F joint-restriction purpose.

Key and essential reasoning: Variance sigma²/Sxx by squared weights and vanishing cross covariances under sampling. df 8, hat-sigma² 4, var 1, se 1, t -2: do not reject under six assumptions. BLUE as above under 1–5; under 1–4 heterogeneous variance unbiasedness survives/consistency under regularity possible, stated BLUE/conventional test not guaranteed. Under1–5/nonnormal BLUE but not stated exact normal/t/F; under 1–6 exact null t/F. Significance not exogeneity/causality; F joint coefficient restrictions. From sigma²/Sxx: doubling noise variance sigma² doubles slope variance and multiplies SE by sqrt(2); doubling Sxx halves slope variance and divides SE by sqrt(2).

Task rubric: apply C1–C4 and the cross-task decision rule below. The proof/definition/condition steps in Explanation steps are the exact shared conceptual key, not optional extra credit. All four components are expressly requested above.

### O005-I2

`item_id: O005-I2`, `item_version: 1`, role: full_capability_check, condition: independent, relation: parallel_variant.

Prompt: Derive variance from disturbance weights and show effect of doubling Sxx. Use n 10, k 1, Sxx 9, SSE 72, slope 3, null 1 to calculate df, sigma², var, se, t and 5% decision(cutoff 2.306). Define BLUE and classify the same three assumption cases: first 4 with heterogeneous variance; first 5 without normality; all 6. Distinguish null-specific inference from exogeneity and identify F purpose. Explain separately how doubling sigma² at fixed Sxx and doubling Sxx at fixed sigma² affect BOTH slope variance and standard error.

Required response components: Weighted-variance derivation with vanishing cross terms and correct noise/regressor-variation effects; BLUE class and first 4/5/6 distinctions stated precisely; Correct df, noise/slope variance, se and null-centered t with conditional decision; Significance/exogeneity distinction and F joint-restriction purpose.

Key and essential reasoning: Variance sigma²/Sxx, cross terms vanish under sample independence; double Sxx halves var/se divided sqrt2. df 8, sigma² 9, var 1, se 1, t(3-1)=2; do not reject null 1 under 6. BLUE precise linear-in-y unbiased conditional-X class under 1–5; first 4 heteroskedastic unbiased/possibly consistent with regularity but theorem/formula not guaranteed; first 5 nonnormal still BLUE/not exact classical t/F; all 6 exact distributions. Significance/null decision cannot establish exogeneity; F joint restrictions. From sigma²/Sxx: doubling noise variance sigma² doubles slope variance and multiplies SE by sqrt(2); doubling Sxx halves slope variance and divides SE by sqrt(2).

Task rubric: apply C1–C4 and the cross-task decision rule below. The proof/definition/condition steps in Explanation steps are the exact shared conceptual key, not optional extra credit. All four components are expressly requested above.

source_units.heading: Rubric and independence
source_units.text:
## Rubric and independence

Pass: all C1–C4 correct, essential reasoning explicit, known independent conditions and fresh item. Partial: one or more components missing, an unexplained claim, or a recoverable arithmetic slip with sound method. Fail: a critical conceptual error, wrong method/assumptions/interpretation, or no usable attempt. Unscorable: unknown conditions/exposure or an alternative outside the prepared key. Equivalent algebra, clear verbal reasoning and synonymous units/assumption names are acceptable; assumption numbers alone are insufficient. Numerical rounding to sensible precision is acceptable. A isolated arithmetic slip is partial and is not treated as established conceptual failure; the learner must independently repair it with a fresh prepared full item before a pass qualifies. No numeric grading scale is invented.

Every full task I1, I2, D1, D2 expressly requests all C1–C4 and has a complete task-specific key plus exact conceptual reasoning above. Omitted pieces are partial even if an unasked answer happens to sound fluent. Supported S and narrow correction C never substitute for a full check.

Permitted acquisition routes: I1+I2; if an item was exposed, failed or unavailable, replace only that full check with a previously unexposed D1 or D2. Any selected pair of distinct items from {I1,I2,D1,D2} covers C1–C4 twice. Do not use an item twice or count a corrected answer to the same item as fresh. D items used immediately are logged as independent replacement checks, not delayed evidence. No shortened variant or arbitrary new task is permitted. Two complete unassisted passes under O005-C1 establish acquisition; they do not establish retention. This is a default evidence rule, not a learner outcome.

Component-to-item coverage on every route:

| Component | S | I1 | I2 | D1 | D2 | Correction C |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | supported | required | required | required | required | narrow repair only |
| C2 | supported | required | required | required | required | narrow repair only |
| C3 | supported | required | required | required | required | narrow repair only |
| C4 | supported | required | required | required | required | narrow repair only |

source_units.heading: Misconceptions and correction
source_units.text:
## Misconceptions and correction

Sign: BLUE means best among every estimator; variance and se confused; t ignores nonzero null; or homoskedasticity confused with normality. Correction: theorem restricts the class; standard error is square root of variance; subtract the null; homoskedasticity concerns spread, normality shape. Hint1: name class and write t numerator. Hint2: calculate residual df and square root explicitly.

Score the original response before help. One ambiguous error only suggests a tentative misconception; establish it only from explicit reasoning or repeated diagnostic signs. Explain the relevant prepared step and its consequence; never label the learner from confidence or a single slip.

### O005-C

`item_id: O005-C`, `item_version: 1`, role: targeted correction; not an acquisition substitute.

Prompt: Fresh O005-C v1: slope 5, null 2, se 1.5. Find t; if MLR1–5 hold but normality unknown, what BLUE/exact-test claims follow?

Key: t 2. BLUE in the conditional linear-unbiased class follows; exact finite-sample t reference is not established without additional normality. Narrow repair only.

Rubric: correct supplied answer plus the exact boundary/reason is a repair pass; omitted reason is partial; repeating the original misconception is fail. Repair success licenses returning to a fresh full prepared item; it never replaces full C1–C4 coverage.

Key and essential reasoning: df 8, sigma² 16, var 1, se 1, t -2, nonrejection under 6. Derivation weighted variances/sampling cross terms/common sigma²; double sigma² doubles var/se×sqrt2. Precise BLUE conditional-X linear unbiased comparison. First 4 heteroskedastic mean preserved/consistency with regularity possible but theorem/test not guaranteed; first 5 nonnormal BLUE not stated exact tests; all 6 exact null t/F. No causality/exogeneity conclusion; F joint restrictions. From sigma²/Sxx: doubling noise variance sigma² doubles slope variance and multiplies SE by sqrt(2); doubling Sxx halves slope variance and divides SE by sqrt(2).

## Prerequisites and checks

### O006-P1

`item_id: O006-P1`, `item_version: 2`, role: prerequisite diagnostic. Capability: O002; reason: Scalar fit/residual arithmetic must be available.

Prompt: Agent-created hypothetical summary, distinct from every full assessment case: mean x=5, mean y=20, Sxx=12, Sxy=-18. Give slope/intercept and define a fitted residual.

Key: Slope $S_{xy}/S_{xx}$=-1.5; intercept 20-(-1.5)*5=27.5; residual is actual y minus fitted y. These probe scalar fit and residual definition only, not the whole O002 outcome.

Rubric: pass requires both coefficients, their stated operations and actual-minus-fitted definition without help; partial for a missing operation/definition or recoverable arithmetic slip; fail for an opposite residual convention or unusable method. Unknown assistance/exposure is unscorable for an independent diagnostic. This distinct focused diagnostic never counts toward acquisition and does not expose O002 or O006 full-item inputs. Ask once before support; never repeat it as fresh evidence. Repair: Return to O002 Explanation2–3 and supported task; full upstream checks remain subject to freshness.

Prepared prerequisite: [[03_Agents/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/lessons/O002.md#Explanation steps]].

### O006-P2

`item_id: O006-P2`, `item_version: 2`, role: prerequisite diagnostic. Capability: O005; reason: Conventional variance/test requires conditions, df and square root.

Prompt: Agent-created hypothetical simple-regression summary, distinct from all full assessment cases: n=12, k=1 nonconstant regressor with intercept, SSE=80, Sxx=20. Give residual df, estimated noise variance, estimated slope variance and standard error. Name the full assumptions needed for the stated exact classical null t reference and its df.

Key: Residual df=n-k-1=10; estimated noise variance=80/10=8; estimated slope variance=8/20=0.4; se=sqrt(0.4), approximately 0.632456. Exact null t(10) requires all six classical assumptions: linearity in parameters, random sampling, no perfect collinearity, zero conditional mean, homoskedasticity and conditional normality. Merely calling residuals orthogonal does not establish the population assumptions. This probes numerical inference prerequisites and the exact-reference condition, not the whole O005 theorem/derivation outcome.

Rubric: pass requires the four calculations with their operations and all six exact-test conditions; partial for a missing calculation/condition or recoverable arithmetic slip; fail for using n as variance df or asserting exact t without normality. Unknown assistance/exposure is unscorable for an independent diagnostic. Ask once before support; this focused item never substitutes for upstream acquisition or exposes its full numerical cases. Repair: Return to O005 Explanation4–6 and supported task, preserving fresh full upstream checks.

Prepared prerequisite: [[03_Agents/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/lessons/O005.md#Explanation steps]].

Adequate qualifying current or explicitly approved compatible evidence permits skipping the matching diagnostic. Otherwise ask each once before targeted support. A focused pass demonstrates only the named dependency components; confidence, familiarity or diagnostic success does not grant upstream whole-objective acquisition or retention. Local foundation failures use the exact explanation here, not an improvised prerequisite curriculum.

source_units.heading: Motivation, intuition, and definitions
source_units.text:
## Motivation, intuition, and definitions

Translate a fare question to a transparent linear model, calculate OLS/predictions/residuals/variance and zero-slope test from a complete summary, and interpret signs/units/domain plus the limits of policy conclusions. The question is what the available information lets us calculate or conclude, and which extra conditions the conclusion needs.

A fare-demand linear specification imposes a constant fitted change per fare unit. Expected negative fare sign is a starting hypothesis, not a source-mandated law. Potential omitted factors include population/density, service quality, car availability, income/driving cost; if they affect demand and co-vary with fare, zero conditional mean can fail. The ten-city table explicitly labels y as passengers per hour(thousand), x dollars: preserve this literal scale even when surprising. The CSV uses undocumented file units and is a separate dataset. Optimal fare requires a defined objective, costs/capacity and credible causal response, absent here.

source_units.heading: Explanation steps
source_units.text:
## Explanation steps

1. Specify travel=beta 0+beta 1*fare+u; interpret slope in y-units per dollar, zero-fare intercept only if relevant. Fix the dataset before calculation; never import CSV units into the table.
2. Obtain mean x, mean y, Sxx, Sxy; divide $S_{xy}/S_{xx}$ and solve intercept. Use fitted difference slope*fare change rather than percentage language for a level-level model.
3. For each city compute fitted and actual-minus-fitted. Check residual sum and fare-weighted residual sum≈0, allowing rounding. These are fitting checks, not assumption evidence.
4. SSE is sum of squared fitted residuals; divide by n -2 for simple regression with intercept. Slope variance estimate=sigma hat²/Sxx; se is square root; t=slope/se for zero null. Under all six assumptions compare |t| to t(n -2); report nonrejection as uncertainty, not proof of no association.
5. Inspect impossible fitted values, very large residuals and intercept extrapolation. The ten-city negative fitted travel at observed fare 1.50 signals linear-specification limitations. It does not license deleting observations. Economic explanations are hypotheses requiring evidence.
6. Interpret the result as sample association unless exogeneity/sampling conditions are supported. Regression alone cannot choose an optimal fare.

source_units.heading: Complete checked-note explanation
source_units.text:
## Complete checked-note explanation

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Transport_Demand_Regression_Seminar.md#From economic intuition to a model]]; fingerprint `8cb7c6b76f548352c216ae9bd1d909a788d8d8f5b8718c2721d23989ce332d7f`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### From economic intuition to a model

Problem 1(i) asks about the sign and shape of demand and other influences. A plausible starting hypothesis is that a higher fare reduces public-transport use, holding relevant alternatives and service conditions fixed. A straight line imposes a constant change in demand per unit price; a curved or logarithmic relation would impose a different shape. The handout leaves the shape to discussion, so the linear model used below is a transparent choice for revising OLS, not a source-mandated demand law. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Seminar 1 OS/Seminar1.pdf#page=1|Seminar 1, PDF p. 1, Problem 1(i)–(iii)]]

An initial specification is

$$
\text{travel}_i=\beta_0+\beta_1\text{price}_i+u_i.
$$

The slope is the change in the model's systematic travel demand associated with a one-unit increase in fare. The intercept is its value at zero fare. Other potential influences include city population and density, service frequency and quality, car availability, income, and the cost of driving. These are economic hypotheses offered to answer the prompt, not variables all observed in the supplied data. If such factors both affect demand and vary systematically with fare, putting them in $u_i$ can violate zero conditional mean. A negative estimated price coefficient alone therefore does not identify a causal demand curve. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Seminar 1 OS/Seminar1.pdf#page=1|Seminar 1, PDF p. 1, Problem 1(i)–(ii)]]; [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=18|Lecture 1, PDF p. 18, exogeneity]]

The manager's ultimate objective is an optimal fare, but the exercise only estimates demand and evaluates the regression. Choosing an optimal fare would additionally require a defined objective, costs or capacity constraints, and a credible estimate of how fare changes affect demand. Those inputs are not supplied; no optimum is claimed here. This limitation follows from the distinction between the manager's motivating question and the tasks actually specified in Problem 1. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Seminar 1 OS/Seminar1.pdf#page=1|Seminar 1, PDF p. 1]]


Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Transport_Demand_Regression_Seminar.md#Ten-city example: keep the source's measurement scale]]; fingerprint `8cb7c6b76f548352c216ae9bd1d909a788d8d8f5b8718c2721d23989ce332d7f`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Ten-city example: keep the source's measurement scale

The printed table labels the dependent variable “Passengers per hour (thousand)” and the fare “Fair price (dollars).” The values below preserve the printed numbers literally. The large passenger scale is not silently corrected. Thus a unit of $y$ means one unit on the table's stated thousand-passengers-per-hour scale, and a unit of price means one dollar. The later CSV has a different numeric scale and no supplied unit dictionary, so its results must not be assigned these table units automatically. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Seminar 1 OS/Seminar1.pdf#page=1|Seminar 1, PDF p. 1, city table]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/assets/seminar1_p1_ten_city_table.png]]

*Source crop: the original ten-city table, including its unit labels. It supplies the observations for the following calculations.* [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Seminar 1 OS/Seminar1.pdf#page=1|Source, PDF p. 1]]

#### Estimate the line

For the ten cities, the calculated sample means and centered sums are

$$
\bar x=0.93,\qquad\bar y=1894,\qquad
S_{xx}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2=1.031,
$$

$$
S_{xy}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)=-3579.7.
$$

Applying the lecture's OLS formula gives

$$
\hat\beta_1=\frac{-3579.7}{1.031}=-3472.065955,
\qquad
\hat\beta_0=1894-(-3472.065955)(0.93)=5123.021339.
$$

Hence $\widehat{\text{travel}}_i=5123.021339-3472.065955\text{price}_i$. A fare difference of \$0.10 is associated with a fitted demand difference of $-347.206596$ units on the printed passenger scale. This is a cross-city association in the chosen linear specification. The estimated intercept is outside the observed fare range, \$0.50–\$1.50, and should not be interpreted as observed demand under a zero-fare policy. Calculations answer Problem 1(iii) using the source table and Lecture 1's centered estimator. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Seminar 1 OS/Seminar1.pdf#page=1|Seminar 1, PDF p. 1]]; [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=15|Lecture 1, PDF p. 15]]

#### Fitted values and residuals

For each city, calculate $\hat y_i$ from the fitted line and subtract it from actual travel: $\hat u_i=y_i-\hat y_i$. Positive residuals mean actual travel exceeds the line's prediction; negative residuals mean actual travel is lower. Rounded results are:

| City | Printed travel | Fare ($) | Fitted travel | Residual |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $C_1$ | 2073 | 0.85 | 2171.765 | −98.765 |
| $C_2$ | 2136 | 0.75 | 2518.972 | −382.972 |
| $C_3$ | 1879 | 0.60 | 3039.782 | −1160.782 |
| $C_4$ | 938 | 1.00 | 1650.955 | −712.955 |
| $C_5$ | 7343 | 0.50 | 3386.988 | 3956.012 |
| $C_6$ | 838 | 0.85 | 2171.765 | −1333.765 |
| $C_7$ | 1648 | 1.00 | 1650.955 | −2.955 |
| $C_8$ | 739 | 0.75 | 2518.972 | −1779.972 |
| $C_9$ | 1071 | 1.50 | −85.078 | 1156.078 |
| $C_{10}$ | 275 | 1.50 | −85.078 | 360.078 |

The fitted line predicts negative travel at \$1.50, illustrating a limitation of this unrestricted linear specification even at an observed fare. The unusually high travel in $C_5$ also leaves a large positive residual. Neither observation licenses deleting a city; both motivate checking specification and omitted factors. This table is an agent calculation from the source observations, answering Problem 1(iv). [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Seminar 1 OS/Seminar1.pdf#page=1|Seminar 1, PDF p. 1]]

#### Disturbance variance, slope variance, and the t statistic

The true disturbances $u_i$ and their variance $\sigma^2$ are unknown. In a simple regression with an intercept, the conventional variance estimator uses $n-2$ residual degrees of freedom:

$$
\hat\sigma^2=\frac{\sum_i\hat u_i^2}{n-2}
=\frac{24{,}075{,}579.500}{8}
=3{,}009{,}447.437.
$$

Two estimated coefficients consume two degrees of freedom. Under the homoskedastic model, the slope's theoretical conditional variance is $\sigma^2/S_{xx}$; replacing the unknown $\sigma^2$ with $\hat\sigma^2$ estimates that variance. The corresponding calculated standard error is

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta_1\mid X)=\frac{\hat\sigma^2}{1.031},
\qquad
\operatorname{se}(\hat\beta_1)=1708.496323.
$$

For $H_0:\beta_1=0$, $t=-3472.065955/1708.496323=-2.032235$. An exact two-sided test compares its absolute value with the appropriate $t_8$ critical value, under the full classical assumptions. At the conventional 5% level it does not reject zero: $|t|$ is below the approximately 2.306 critical value. This does not prove no relationship; ten observations and substantial residual variation leave considerable uncertainty. The formulas and computation are the worked solution to the handout's variance and $t$-statistic tasks, interpreted using the lecture's inference statement. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/Seminar 1 OS/Seminar1.pdf#page=1|Seminar 1, PDF pp. 1–2, Problem 1(iv)]]; [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Econometrics_II/Week_1/2026_Lecture1_print.pdf#page=26|Lecture 1, PDF p. 26]]

## Worked example

O006-W v1, note-grounded ten-city values: n 10, mean x=0.93, mean y 1894, Sxx 1.031, Sxy -3579.7. Slope -3472.065955/intercept 5123.021339; a $0.10 difference predicts -347.206596 printed y-units. At C1 fare 0.85, actual 2073, fitted 2171.765 and residual -98.765; at 1.50 fitted -85.078. SSE 24075579.500 gives sigma hat² 3009447.437; se 1708.496323; t -2.032235, df 8. Under maintained six assumptions, |t|<2.306 gives5% nonrejection. Ten observations/noise leave uncertainty. The zero-fare intercept lies outside 0.50–1.50. ## Practice with fading assistance

For S, show the setup and allow reference to Explanation steps; ask the learner to supply the missing calculations/decisions and reasons before feedback.
